### The own checker makes a division or product of equal operands one value: a functional-consistency lemma before any circuit is built

[`6213df4c793e`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/6213df4c793efb8db87c1bcd5a64f1af649232db) · [log `f67e8c835e0a`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3761db96-b870-47f7-aded-2ba264c165f4/f67e8c835e0a9e3fd91473191d986f0eef13e83a52620ff2b8a981fb5cf29d11.jsonl.gz)

The own checker leaves divisions and multiplications to the solver as fresh bits under facts, and shares one only when its operand terms are identical. Two operations on equal values written differently (Math.abs(hash) % n and (hash & 0x7fffffff) % n, for a hash that is not negative) were separate unknowns, so the solver answered them differently, each model was refined, both 32-bit dividers were built, and the solver was left proving two dividers equivalent: benchmark case real/bucket/fix-confined ran out of time (over 100 s; 20 s deadline: 2 of 2 divisions built, 53,649 clauses).

Now, when a model gives two operations of one kind and width equal operands (a product's in either order) but different results, bits.rs adds the lemma (a1 == a2 && b1 == b2) -> (q1 == q2 && r1 == r2) and solves again, before refining any operation (Blaster::inconsistent_pair, add_congruence; the engine's solve loop). The lemma holds of every real operation, so it rules out no real execution; for a division by zero, whose bits nothing reads, it only picks equal values.

### Confirming a proof that rests on contracts: under --confirm, JBMC applies the own checker's contracts at the same calls and proves it again

[`c792ec25564f`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/c792ec25564f07fc5f91c54302ccbd7502feb262) · [log `261e85d7b862`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3761db96-b870-47f7-aded-2ba264c165f4/261e85d7b8624a58d58746c317c21b709baa77f38ad2e74720230fcb211be8e8.jsonl.gz)

Under --engine auto --confirm, a proof of the own checker that rests on contracts for gaps (--gaps advised) was not sent to JBMC: the confirmation was not-asked, with the reason 'JBMC cannot apply' a contract, untrue since JBMC applies contracts by rewriting call sites (step 4c, part two). equivalence::confirm now takes the contracts (ConfirmContracts: the gap setting, the directories whose call sites are rewritten, the class path, a directory): it reads JBMC's goto program, applies the same contracts with jbmc_contracts::apply, runs JBMC on the rewritten class path, holds its proof to what it still approximates under the own checker's gap mode, and settles the contract records. A confirmed proof says it rests on the same contracts, by id. Gaps assumed under --gaps assume stay not-asked; a gap JBMC has that no contract closes gives no verdict.

A confirmation checks the reasoning given the contracts, not the contracts, whose evidence (proved, tested, trusted) the verdict states. Both drivers pass the contracts; lib/README.md describes it, and the sound-verdicts brief records the user's decisions and the group 2 review as done.

An outside review of the repository at 6cea609e (kept verbatim as llm-dlc/loops/engine-priorities-review.md) read the raw benchmark results of job 20261106-102624 and the JBMC jobs' outputs, and changes the draft's direction. Its figures were rechecked against lib/benchmark/results.json. Case by case, the own checker alone decides 10 cases correctly under strict and JBMC alone 3. The own checker was faster on all 98 cases both decided correctly. JBMC's [0:20] and [-100000:100000] stages take about 30 s of binary search's 58.6 s and of 141's 65.2 s, and 15 s of floor-mod's 15.5 s, where the full range finds its counterexample in 0.25 s. The JBMC phase table counts time twice: CBMC times Runtime Post-process inside Runtime Solver, and phases.rs adds one to encoding and the other to solving (held/reverse's phases add up to 22.0 s against 15.9 s of wall time). The three cases only JBMC wins are all application &lt;clinit>s.\n\nThe draft, renamed llm-dlc/loops/engine-priorities.md and still not a brief, now plans: (1) exclusive JBMC phases, solver identity recorded, a strict rerun saving gap_table.py's output; (2) a job comparing today's staged search, full range first, and one tightly budgeted stage; (3) application class initializers in the own checker, counted before implementing, then a native/JBMC coverage inventory; (4) the root cause of the two JBMC witnesses that don't reproduce (caught/1, nestedHandler/1); (5) captured incremental queries and a narrow SAT interface before solver experiments; (6) contracts for example 071's two property proofs. The fork candidates are deferred. Old instructions are dropped rather than kept, at the user's request. Links in sound-verdicts.md and lib/benchmark/README.md point at the new file; the README notes the overcount. Documents only, nothing run.

### engine-priorities.md folds example 071's work into Phase 3 as JDK models for Enum.&lt;init>, List.of and List.copyOf

Example 071's first two property proofs, and 013's, reach JBMC stubs for Enum.&lt;init>(String, int), List.of and List.copyOf, all called through Quorum's Decision type and its enums, so strict turns those proofs into no verdict. Contracts can't close these well: with object parameters they can only be trusted, which is below the proved-or-tested bar for CI, and they can be false in general (List.of throws on a null element). So Phase 3 now adds exact models in lib/models instead: Enum.&lt;init> sets name and ordinal; the immutable list keeps null rejection, refusal of changes, and copyOf's identity. The check is 071 and 013 rerun under strict. The separate Phase 6 is removed. Contracts over complex objects, and other ways of verifying them, move to a new Deferred section to revisit in a later loop. Also corrects the evidence: 071 reaches all three stubs, as 013 does. ### A stopped feature loop continues by running the same command again

[`b616ee59fb2b`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/b616ee59fb2bd854857aa30c4caa16cbf533e6f3) · [log `71958bec8e62`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3761db96-b870-47f7-aded-2ba264c165f4/71958bec8e6298da2d91c6971e9dbc196b093012a5ff66799f49ca3ba6bb94f6.jsonl.gz)

feature-loop.sh's instruction for a brief used to send the session to the next piece of work that 'this run's earlier commits' had not done. A restart sets a new starting change, so after one that list is empty, and nothing made the session look at changes an interrupted cycle left in the working copy, which the next commit could then sweep into unrelated work. Each cycle now first runs jj status, and finishes, verifies and commits a change left there (or says in the commit why it sets it aside). It then takes the next piece of work by the brief's Progress section, which carries over between runs, as well as this run's commits. The header comment and llm-dlc/README.md say that the restart is the same command, and to leave no other work uncommitted when starting. Verified with bash -n and by expanding the instruction for engine-priorities.md and reading it.

### A feature-loop cycle finishes only its own interrupted work and keeps other sessions' files out of its commit

[`7c20157e29b0`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/7c20157e29b0d5f067f5d09eff1e2295f3a8b67f) · [log `7a93fb04e657`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3761db96-b870-47f7-aded-2ba264c165f4/7a93fb04e6576015d0dd03a5adefbfc8851252bdeb9a1e33ecda85b60d09ac77.jsonl.gz)

Following the previous commit, a cycle treated any change in the working copy as its own interrupted work. That would be wrong while the verification loop or another session has files there uncommitted, and sync.py commit commits the whole working copy. Each cycle now runs jj status and judges what a change is. One that belongs to the brief's current step, by its Progress section or the session's own last turn, is finished, verified and committed, and that is the cycle's piece of work. Anything else is another session's: it is left alone, never finished, reverted or discarded, and kept out of the cycle's commit by moving it below and back, as step 5 of .claude/skills/run-verification/SKILL.md already does the other way round. The header comment and llm-dlc/README.md are updated to match. Verified with bash -n and by expanding the instruction for engine-priorities.md and reading it.

### run-streams.sh starts a brief's parallel streams in one terminal, each forked from the compacted planning session

llm-dlc/tools/run-streams.sh engines, run from the default workspace, sets up and runs the engine-priorities streams. The first time, it compacts the brief's own session (the conversation that planned the streams) once and adds the jj workspaces ../REPO-jbmc and ../REPO-native from @-. It then runs feature-loop.sh engines-jbmc and engines-native from their workspaces side by side, each line prefixed with its stream. If the planning session's transcript is missing (it ran on another machine), it says where to copy it.

feature-loop.sh reads a new '- fork: SESSION' brief setting. A session with no transcript yet starts as a fork of that one (claude --resume PARENT --fork-session --session-id ID), in a first turn with tools and project settings off. The parent's transcript is copied into the workspace's project directory for the fork and removed after it, so the repo's hooks never sync it there, where it would be published as a second copy. Both stream briefs fork from 3761db96 and drop their 2.5 GB caps (they will run on a larger machine, cvm, under the default 3.5 GB each). The main brief, llm-dlc/README.md and the run-verification skill describe it.

### copy-session.sh moves a session to another machine, and the reconcile loop starts fresh with a map of the streams' work

[`5c060f24322f`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/5c060f24322f86ad2ac86c1819ae74edaa7736e1) · [log `a42086f02b16`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3761db96-b870-47f7-aded-2ba264c165f4/a42086f02b16680ee418c6190177c70ab0f901b69ab180c6c41509d9eb0c7927.jsonl.gz)

llm-dlc/tools/copy-session.sh HOST SESSION (id or unique prefix), run after closing a session, moves it to another machine. It refuses a session that is live (a claude process names it, or its transcript changed in the last minute) and publishes with sync.py push --bookmark main (--no-push skips that). It copies the transcript and the session's directory into HOST's Claude Code project directory for the repo, under a temporary name with a checksum check, and refuses to overwrite a different transcript there. Then it moves the local transcript to ~/.claude/moved-sessions/, so the session goes on on one machine only: a push from here republishes every session it finds and would roll back one that grew on HOST (--keep-local keeps it). It exists to take the planning session 3761db96 to cvm, where run-streams.sh forks the streams from it.

The engine-priorities brief's own loop, which merges the streams, now starts from a fresh session (c2bd9df4) instead of resuming the planning session. Reconcile step 2 now refuses to commit a stream's uncommitted work, since that means an interrupted cycle. run-streams.sh takes the session to compact and fork from the stream briefs' '- fork:' (which must agree), no longer from the main brief.

Verified with fake ssh and scp running against a local fake remote home. Each case behaved as intended: refusing a just-written transcript and one a claude process names, copying the transcript and its directory with matching checksums, retiring the local copy with a .moved note, refusing a different remote transcript, and --keep-local. run-streams.sh rerun in a throwaway jj repo with a fake claude: a missing planning transcript stops it, otherwise one compact and two forks from 3761db96, then both loops.

### run-streams.sh runs a brief's whole loop unattended: streams, jobs, then the merge

[`7dca2d9d176c`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/7dca2d9d176c92cdf2398ea9e1122d91984e7406) · [log `ece0b699a5ab`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3761db96-b870-47f7-aded-2ba264c165f4/ece0b699a5ab9ec790e7136da645218ef71500e5f2c2fa16e3aaa20927b40e80.jsonl.gz)

llm-dlc/tools/run-streams.sh engines now needs a person only at the end. After the compact, forks and workspaces, it starts verification-loop.sh (unless one already runs for this repo) so the loops' jobs are run, collected and committed. It runs both streams' loops and supervises each. When every stream is finished, it runs the brief's own loop (feature-loop.sh engines, the merge, in its fresh session) the same way, then stops the verification loop and exits.

The supervisor reads a status line that each brief now ends its Progress with: '- Status: working', 'waiting on jobs ID ...', 'done' or 'blocked: ...'. All three engine-priorities briefs carry the rule and start at 'working'. A loop waiting on jobs is run again once each job's result is collected under verification/results/, polling every RUN_STREAMS_POLL seconds (300) and giving up as blocked after RUN_STREAMS_JOB_WAIT (12 h). Done or blocked, it is finished, and a blocked stream is merged with what it committed. A stop with no such status is retried once, then counted as blocked; so is one claiming to wait on jobs that are already back. On a restart, finished loops are skipped and waiting ones wait first. verification-loop.sh gains a stop on SIGUSR1, which lets the run under way finish. The brief's Streams and Reconciling text and llm-dlc/README.md describe it.

Verified with a dry run in a throwaway jj repo, with a fake claude that sets status lines and commits and a fake verification loop that collects a job after a few seconds. In order: one compact and two forks; jbmc waited on its job, picked up when it was collected and finished; native finished; the merge loop ran and finished; the verification loop stopped on SIGUSR1; exit 0. A restart skipped the finished stream. Ctrl-C mid-cycle gave exit 130, both stream loops recorded the interruption, and no process or scope was left. The verification-loop detection first matched the test shell's own command line; it now needs a bash running the script with the repo as its working directory.

I measured `fix-confined` with a 20 s deadline and it confirms the theory. Both analyses are below; you said you'd decide from them.

## 1. `real/bucket/fix-confined` runs out of time

**What happens.** The two versions are `Math.abs(hash) % buckets` and `(hash & 0x7fffffff) % buckets`, with `hash < 0` excluded by the scope. The run took 3 paths and 6 solver calls, and **both divisions were built in full (2 of 2)**. Then the solver timed out on about 53,600 clauses.

**Why.** For a non-negative hash, both dividends equal `hash`, but they are different terms. The own checker gives each division fresh quotient and remainder bits, constrained only by general facts about division, and it shares a division only when its operand terms are identical. So nothing says "equal operands give equal results." The solver picks different remainders for equal dividends. Each model is caught as wrong, the division circuit is built, and the solver is left proving two 32-bit dividers equivalent. That is a classically hard problem for a SAT solver.

**The fix.** Add functional consistency (an Ackermann lemma) to the refinement loop in `bmc/bits.rs`:
- When a model gives two divisions, or two multiplications, equal operand values but different results, add the clause (a₁ = a₂ ∧ b₁ = b₂) → (q₁ = q₂ ∧ r₁ = r₂) before building any circuit.
- Here the solver then only has to show `hash & 0x7fffffff == hash` for `hash ≥ 0`, which is trivial. Neither divider would be built.

### 20. 2026-11-06 14:37 UTC

> Let's review questions interactively except order (save that for last), when done summarize the proposed order and any tradeoff decisions for me to consider, then we will review that and create our brief

**Reply:**

The answers are recorded in `engine-priorities.md` and committed with 0 errors. Nothing is pushed.

## What you decided
- **Staging:** if the job shows full range first is faster, only JBMC's default changes. The own checker keeps its stages per violating path. Witnesses stay small either way, because `lib/src/shrink.rs` already shrinks a JBMC counterexample through the interpreter.
- **Class initializers:** count first, then choose a scope, leaning toward the most common semantics where that's convenient.
- **Solvers:** Bitwuzla is the preferred backend, because it sits on CaDiCaL and makes a bigger architecture change easy to try. A newer CaDiCaL, Z3 or cvc5 come in only if a quick estimate shows more than a small gain.

## Proposed order
1. **Measurements first (small):**
   - Count JBMC's phases without overlap, using fixtures from real JBMC output for a success, a timeout and an out-of-memory run.
   - Record which SAT solver each engine used.

### 21. 2026-11-06 14:45 UTC

> Elaborate on what Exampple 071 work entails

**Reply:**

## Example 071, the work involved

**What it is.** A B11 property proof on Quorum's `VoteRule#grant`. JBMC checks three properties:
1. With the same term and the vote already given to someone else, the vote is refused. Proved.
2. When the candidate's term is older, the vote is refused. Proved.
3. When the candidate's log is behind, the vote is refused. Refuted. This is the bug the example plants, and the witness replays.

Under strict, properties 1 and 2 become no verdict. Property 3 stands, so the example's verdict (a violation) doesn't move. What's lost is the half of the example that shows the property holding where it should.

**Where the gaps come from.** Everything comes from Quorum's shared `Decision` type, not from `VoteRule` itself:
- `decide` returns `transition(FOR_THE_CANDIDATE, GRANT)`, which calls `List.of(effects)`.
- The `Transition` record's constructor calls `List.copyOf(effects)`.
- The four enums (`TermOrder`, `Ballot`, `LogOrder`, `VoteEffect`) call `Enum.<init>(String, int)` from their initializers.

JBMC has no bytecode for any of these three, so it stubs them, and strict refuses the stubs. Example 013 reaches the same three. I had that wrong in the draft, which said only 013 reaches `Enum.<init>`. The draft is fixed now, but the fix isn't committed yet.

**Two ways to recover the proofs:**

**A. Contracts under `--gaps advised`.** These would be cheap to write, but they would only be *trusted*.

### 25. 2026-11-06 15:21 UTC

> Before we run, confirm what behaviour would happen if feature loop stopped? Ideally we could just run a continue command and it would pick up exactly where it left off with no changes (unsure if this behaviour is default).

**Reply:**

There's no separate "continue" command. Running the same command again is how you continue, and in most cases it picks up where it stopped. Here is what happens, from reading `feature-loop.sh`.

**Why rerunning works.** The brief fixes the session id, so every run resumes this same session with its full transcript. Each cycle's commit also updates the brief's Progress section with what it did and what comes next. A new run reads the brief again, Progress included, and takes the next piece from there.

**How each kind of stop behaves:**

| How it stopped | State left | What a rerun does |
|---|---|---|
| A cycle made no commit, or the stop/continue answer was unclear | The session is **not compacted**, so the context of what went wrong is kept | Resumes with that context. You may want to read the session first, since this stop means it may need you |
| You type `0` or `stop` | The cycle finishes, commits and compacts first | Clean continue from Progress |
| The session decides it's done, or the cycles run out | Commits are in, a summary is written to `llm-dlc/loop-summaries/` | Starts again, and will probably decide again that it's done |
| The brief changed (an edit outside Progress) | Stops before the next cycle | Reads the new brief. This is by design |
